summaries.example: Imagine the word “dodo.” The sentence “A dodo lived” can be true because dodos lived long ago. But “A dodo lives” is false if it says that a dodo is alive now. Medieval thinkers studied how words can keep a general meaning while pointing to different things in different sentences. They also noticed that a word can talk about itself: “Cat has three letters” talks about the word, not an animal.
summaries.summary: Medieval philosophers developed a detailed theory called the properties of terms. They wanted to explain how words and phrases work in statements, especially how statements can be true or false and how arguments can succeed or fail. One important distinction was between signification, a term’s general meaning, and supposition, what that term stands for in a particular use. For example, “man” could have a general meaning while different uses of it stand for different people. Medieval writers also described material supposition, when a word stands for itself; simple supposition, often connected with a form or universal; and personal supposition, when it stands for ordinary individual things. They studied how words such as past-tense verbs can widen a term’s range, called ampliation, or how adjectives and other expressions can narrow it, called restriction. They also examined appellation, or how a predicate applies to things, and relation, especially words such as “he” or “himself” that refer back to earlier expressions. These ideas developed from the twelfth through the sixteenth centuries. No single medieval account stayed unchanged, and the terms do not match modern semantic concepts exactly.
key_ideas: Medieval philosophers built a theory about how terms work in sentences.
They separated a word’s general meaning from what it stands for on a particular occasion.
Different sentence patterns can make the same word point to different things.
Their ideas were used to explain truth, mistakes in reasoning, and fallacies.
The theory changed over many centuries, and different thinkers did not always agree.
summaries.why_it_matters: This topic shows that questions about language are not new. Medieval thinkers carefully asked what a word means, what it points to, and how a sentence changes its reach. Their work helps us notice why a small change in tense, adjective, or pronoun can change an argument. It also teaches us to be careful when comparing older theories with modern ideas: they may resemble one another without being identical.

important_terms.definition: What a word means in a general way, before we look at how it is being used in a particular sentence.
What a word points to or stands for in a particular sentence.
Using a word to talk about the word, its sound, or its written form.
A change that makes a word cover more possible things, such as past or future things.
A change that makes a word cover fewer things, such as when “white” narrows “animal” to white animals.

questions_to_think_about: Can one word have the same meaning but point to different things?
When does a sentence talk about a word instead of what the word usually names?
How can a past-tense verb change what a sentence is about?

summaries.example: Consider the argument: “Man is the worthiest of creatures. Socrates is a man. Therefore, Socrates is the worthiest of creatures.” Medieval logicians could diagnose the error by saying that “man” has different kinds of supposition in the two premises. In the first, it can stand for a universal or form; in the second, it stands for an individual person. The repeated word therefore does not function as one unambiguous middle term. A related distinction appears in “A noun has four letters” versus “A noun is a part of speech”: in the first, “noun” is used materially, to discuss the linguistic item; in the second, it is used personally, to discuss nouns as things in language.
summaries.summary: The medieval theory of the properties of terms was a developing semantic theory designed to account for truth, fallacy, and inference. Its central distinction was between signification and supposition. Signification was usually understood as a term’s general semantic content and was prior to its particular uses. Supposition concerned what an occurrence of the term stood for within a proposition. This distinction was not stable across all authors. Earlier writers often connected signification with a form or universal and supposition with individuals; Ockham’s nominalist approach instead treated signification extensionally, as concerning things of which a term can truly be predicated, while universals were understood through mental acts or linguistic items. Supposition had several modes. Material supposition involved reference to a word or expression itself. Simple supposition was often associated with a universal or form, although Ockham explained it differently. Personal supposition involved ordinary objects and was divided into discrete and common forms, including determinate, confused and distributive modes. Medieval logicians used valid and invalid descent between general propositions and propositions about individual “inferiors” to characterize these modes. They also discussed copulation, especially the predicative function of adjectives and verbs, though this distinction was increasingly absorbed into supposition. Ampliation widened a term’s range to include past, future, possible, or merely intelligible objects; restriction narrowed it. Ockham rejected the usual treatment of ampliation in several cases, analyzing propositions as ambiguous instead. Appellation concerned the application of predicates and, in some accounts, the forms or concepts associated with them.
key_ideas: The theory of properties of terms was a semantic framework for analyzing truth, fallacy, and inference.
Signification was generally treated as independent of a term’s particular occurrence, while supposition concerned its use in a proposition.
Medieval authors distinguished material, simple, and personal supposition, though they disagreed about how these should be understood.
Modes of common personal supposition were analyzed through determinate, confused, and distributive patterns, often using ascent and descent.
Ampliation and restriction explain how tense, modality, predicates, and other expressions widen or narrow a term’s range.
The framework evolved: some properties were absorbed into supposition, and different authors, including Ockham, offered competing semantic accounts.
summaries.why_it_matters: The entry matters because it presents a sophisticated historical attempt to explain how language functions inside reasoning. Its distinctions anticipate some modern concerns about meaning, reference, extension, quantification, quotation, modality, and anaphora, but the correspondence is only partial. Studying the differences prevents simplistic historical translation. It also shows how semantic theories respond to practical problems: ambiguous terms, invalid syllogisms, changing temporal or modal contexts, and pronouns whose reference depends on an antecedent. The theory’s long development illustrates that philosophical systems can be revised as new logical problems become important.

important_terms.definition: A term’s general semantic content, treated by many medieval authors as prior to its use in a particular proposition.
The way an occurrence of a term is taken to stand for particular objects, forms, or other items in a proposition; its modes vary by context.
Supposition in which a term stands for a linguistic expression or for itself, rather than for what it ordinarily signifies.
Supposition for ordinary objects falling under a term’s meaning; it is often contrasted with material and simple supposition.
A widening of a term’s range, for example through past tense, modal language, or expressions concerning possible objects.
A narrowing of a term’s range through a predicate, adjective, possessive, tense, or other part of a proposition.
A property concerning how a predicate applies to its subjects or to the form associated with what it predicates.
The behavior of a relative expression, such as “he” or “himself,” in referring back to an antecedent and taking a corresponding supposition.

questions_to_think_about: If a word’s signification stays constant, what explains its different suppositions in separate propositions?
Does “simple supposition” require belief in real universals, or can it be explained in a nominalist theory?
Why might “A white thing was black” receive different analyses under an ampliative account and Ockham’s ambiguity-based account?
How does “Every man sees himself” differ logically from “Every man sees every man”?
Are these medieval categories best understood as theories of meaning, reference, inference, truth conditions, or a combination?

summaries.example: Suppose someone says, “A dodo lived,” and then concludes, “A dodo lives.” The word “dodo” has not changed its general meaning, but the two sentences use it differently because the past and present tenses affect what it can stand for. Medieval logicians called this kind of error a fallacy connected with univocation: a speaker treats a word as if its reference stayed the same when it did not. Another example is “The word ‘dog’ has three letters.” Here the sentence is about the word itself, not about dogs. This is material supposition.
summaries.summary: Medieval philosophers developed the theory of the properties of terms to study how language works in logical statements. They were especially interested in explaining when a sentence is true, why an argument goes wrong, and how a fallacy can hide inside an apparently reasonable use of words. Signification was usually treated as a term’s general meaning, while supposition concerned what that term stood for in a particular proposition. For instance, “man” could retain a general meaning while one use stood for one set of men and another use stood for a different set. Writers described several kinds of supposition. Material supposition occurs when a word is being used to talk about itself. Simple supposition was often connected with a universal or form, although nominalists such as Ockham rejected real universals and explained the category differently. Personal supposition is the ordinary case in which a term stands for individual objects. It could be determinate or confused, with further distinctions involving whether a statement ranges over some or all of the relevant objects. Medieval authors also studied how terms are widened by ampliation and narrowed by restriction. Past tense could allow a term to include former objects; modal expressions could include possible objects; adjectives could limit a term to a smaller group. Appellation concerned how predicates apply, while relation concerned expressions that refer back to an antecedent. These categories developed across several centuries, and their meanings shifted. They resemble modern ideas such as meaning, reference, extension, quotation, and anaphora, but no medieval property exactly equals a modern one.
key_ideas: Medieval theories of terms were meant to explain meaning, truth, inference, and fallacies together.
A term’s signification and its supposition are related but not identical.
Terms can stand for words, universals or forms, and individual objects in different contexts.
Predicates, tense, modality, and other expressions can change the range of a term.
Relative words such as “he” and “himself” create special problems because they refer back to earlier terms.
The theory changed from the twelfth century onward, so there was no single permanent medieval definition of every property.
summaries.why_it_matters: This subject matters because it shows how much careful reasoning can depend on ordinary words. A sentence may become misleading when a term shifts from talking about a word to talking about objects, or when tense and adjectives change the group under discussion. Medieval thinkers also demonstrate that philosophical vocabulary evolves: later writers reorganized earlier categories, and different schools gave competing explanations. Their work can help students read arguments more carefully while also reminding us not to force historical theories into modern categories.

important_terms.definition: The general meaning or content associated with a term, apart from one particular sentence in which it appears.
What a term stands for in a particular sentence or argument. The same term may have different suppositions in different uses.
When a term stands for a word, sound, or written expression rather than for the things it normally names.
When a general term stands for a form or universal, in theories that accept such entities or meanings.
When a term stands for ordinary individual things, such as people or animals.
Widening the group a term can stand for, often because of past tense, possibility, or words about belief.
Narrowing the group a term can stand for, often because of an adjective, predicate, or possessive phrase.
The way a predicate applies to the things under discussion; the meaning of this term changed across medieval theories.

questions_to_think_about: Why is “The word ‘dog’ has three letters” different from “A dog has four legs”?
Can a word have one meaning while standing for different people or objects in different sentences?
Should “A white thing was black” have one broad meaning or two different readings?
Why might “he” not be replaceable by the full noun phrase that came before it?
Which seems more important for understanding an argument: what words mean generally or what they stand for in that argument?
